Warren H. Oven
Alternatives to this development have been considered in the Draft Environmental Impact Statement. Host of those alternatives involve some type of additional power generation which for economic and, at times, environmental reasons are undesirable. The only nongeneration alternative considered was that of conservation and rate revision. Duke Power had no consideration of conservation and rate revision as an alternative in Section 8.2 of its application for license before the FPC. The FPC could not determine quantitatively the effects of such measures and/or the price elasticity of demand. Therefore, the FPC dismissed conservation and rate revision as a reasonable alternative while urging the vigorous pursuit of such measures. I submit that if this development were built and such measures were successful, the land would still have the impact and the Company would have an unnecessary investment.
From Exhibit 1 in the application for license, data is given that supports the following conclusions. This facility is capable of continuous full load operation for 32 hours. The continuous pumpback to full pond will require 45 hours. Therefore, each 32,000 MMH of electricity generated will require 45,000 MMH of pumpback energy with a resulting efficiency of 71.1%. Annual total operating time will be 7000 hours. Approximately 2500 hours of that time will represent peneration on demand at the full rated capacity. The plant will therefore be in some phase of full capacity operation for approximately 80% of the year. The annual pumpback time will be equivalent to 4500 hours or approximately 100 complete pumpback cycles. With 13,000 MMH wasted on each pumpback, the result will be an annual waste of 1,300,000 MMH of electricity.
On the basis of the average consumption per household listed for Duke Pover's customers through October 31, 1974, the annual waste at Bad Creek would provide one month's electrical energy for 1,454,545.4 homes. On the same basis the annual waste at Bad Creek would provide for the total annual consumption for 121,212.1 homes. There were 951,459 residential customers on January 1, 1975.
To put this in mother perspective, the annual waste at Bad Creek represents 84.3% of the total annual generation of Duke Power conventional hydro units at median streamflow conditions. In other words, neglecting the lands inundated by smaller impoundments and based on the total surface acreages for impoundments on the Catawba River and Lake Keowee, the waste at Bad Creek will negate the hydroelectrical benefit for which 83,174 acres of land were flooded.
The conflict is obvious. The more Bad Creek operates the more energy is vasted. The less it operates the more difficult to justify economically.
